title: Compassion can be trained
hook: short programs at Stanford and Emory measured gains in compassion

segments.voice: Yesterday: care for carers. The people who look after others need looking after too. Did a thank-you go out? Day one thousand three hundred six.

She's just a kind person. People say it the way they'd say someone is tall, or left-handed. A fixed fact. Some people got the warm heart, some got the cool head, and that's the hand you're dealt. It's a comfortable idea, especially on a day you weren't kind at all. But two university programs put it to a test. They didn't ask whether some people are kinder than others. They asked a different question: if ordinary adults practiced compassion on purpose, for a short stretch, would anything change?
screen: `SHE'S JUST A KIND PERSON.` → `A HAND YOU'RE DEALT?` → `A DIFFERENT QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the programs. At Stanford, a course called Compassion Cultivation Training was developed by Thupten Jinpa, a scholar and longtime translator for the Dalai Lama. At Emory, a program called Cognitively-Based Compassion Training was developed by Lobsang Tenzin Negi, who teaches at Emory. Both draw on Tibetan Buddhist practice, taught in plain language, with no requirement to be Buddhist. Second, what they practice. Steadying attention. Wishing yourself well. Then widening the circle: someone you love, a stranger, someone difficult, and eventually everyone. Ordinary exercises, done in class and at home. Third, what was measured. Researchers studying the Stanford course reported that people who finished it scored higher on their own reports of compassion, for others and for themselves. Studies of the Emory program reported changes too, in measures such as reading other people's emotions from their faces. The gains reported were modest, and some rest on what people say about themselves; the researchers name limits like these. Still, in these studies, something moved. Fourth, an old claim. The Chinese philosopher Mencius, in the book that carries his name, taught that all people have a heart that can't bear to see others suffer, and that the feeling of commiseration is a beginning of goodness, like a fire that has just caught or a spring that has just begun to flow. A beginning isn't the finished thing. Mencius said it has to be developed. That's the whole idea in one picture. Compassion isn't only a trait you have or don't. It's also a skill you can practice. Trainable.
screen: `STANFORD AND EMORY: TWO COURSES.` · `WIDENING THE CIRCLE.` · then, large: `SOMETHING MOVED.` · then: `MENCIUS: A BEGINNING TO DEVELOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: five minutes of compassion, starting now and finishing later if you like. Sit and settle. First, someone easy to love: picture them, and hold one quiet wish, may you be well. Then a stranger you saw this week: the same wish. Then yourself: the same wish, without arguing with it. Stay with whichever face is in mind when the bell ends. If you want the full five minutes, carry on after it rings. The bell holds the time.
Compassion can be trained. Short courses at Stanford and Emory reported modest gains, and Mencius called the feeling a beginning that has to be developed. Today's word.
Your line: trainable. Today, when you catch yourself thinking you're just not that kind of person, add one word: yet. Then offer one stranger the quiet wish. Day one thousand three hundred six.

howItsDone: Secular compassion courses drawn from Tibetan Buddhist practice, such as Stanford's Compassion Cultivation Training and Emory's Cognitively-Based Compassion Training, teach people to widen a circle of goodwill from loved ones to strangers to everyone; in Confucian thought, Mencius taught that the feeling of commiseration must be developed.

notes: Confirm: Compassion Cultivation Training was developed at Stanford by Thupten Jinpa; Cognitively-Based Compassion Training at Emory by Lobsang Tenzin Negi.

Confirm the Stanford study reported increases in self-reported compassion for others and self-compassion, and that an Emory CBCT study reported improved empathic accuracy (reading emotions from faces/eyes).
Course lengths (in weeks) are left out under the claims rule.

Mencius 2A:6 is paraphrased (commiseration as the beginning of benevolence; the four beginnings must be developed). 'Sprout' is a common rendering of the image; Legge's wording differs, so nothing is quoted. Confirm the summary is fair.
